title: 1 Corinthians
subtitle: Paul to a proud, divided church in a Roman harbor city
lead: First Corinthians is Paul's answer to a church he founded in the Greek city of Corinth and left some time before. News had reached him in Ephesus from Chloe's people of quarrels, and the Corinthians had written him a letter of their own with questions. He answers both, point by point: factions over teachers, a man living with his father's wife, lawsuits between believers, sex and marriage, food offered to idols, behavior at worship and at the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, love, and the resurrection of the dead.

It is the most practical of Paul's letters and the best picture we have of an early Christian church at work, with its money, its social ranks, its meals, its worship and its mistakes. It holds some of the best-known passages in the New Testament (the word of the cross in 1:18-25, the hymn to love in chapter 13, the creed of 15:3-8) and some of the most debated (head coverings, women in worship, tongues, baptism for the dead). This Plain, like the rest of the site, gives each view its strongest form and shows where the churches differ.
facts: Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender (1:1). Almost every scholar accepts the letter as Paul's own.

Written from Ephesus (16:8, 19), in the 50s AD, some time after Paul left Corinth. A letter of the emperor Claudius found at Delphi, dated to AD 52, names Gallio as proconsul (Acts 18:12), which anchors the date of Paul's stay in Corinth in the early 50s.
Corinth, a Roman colony refounded in 44 BC, capital of the province of Achaia, with two harbors and the Isthmian Games.
A letter, answering both a report from Chloe's people (1:11) and a letter from Corinth (7:1), with many topics taken in turn.
Greek, in a vigorous style that uses the rhetoric of its day.
authorship: 1 Corinthians is one of the seven letters almost all scholars accept as Paul's, with Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Sosthenes (1:1) is a co-sender, but from 1:4 the letter speaks in Paul's voice, and at 16:21 he writes the closing greeting "with my own hand."

Paul says he had written an earlier letter (5:9). It is lost. 1 Corinthians is thus not the first letter to Corinth, and what we call 2 Corinthians is also not the second: Paul seems to refer to a painful visit and a "tearful letter" between the two (2 Corinthians 2:1-4; 7:8).

Some scholars (Johannes Weiss, Walter Schmithals, and others) have divided 1 Corinthians into two or more letters because of shifts of topic and tone, for example between 1:10-4:21 and the chapters on conduct and worship. Most scholars, among them Margaret Mitchell, hold the letter together, seeing one plan: an appeal for unity (1:10) that runs through every section. Chapters 1-4 are rarely thought to be separate.

Two passages are suspected by some of being later insertions: 11:3-16 (head coverings) and 14:34-35 (women silent). They are treated at those verses. Few scholars doubt chapters 1-4, though William O. Walker has doubted 2:6-16 and some have suggested that 4:6 is a later note.

audience.to: The church of God in Corinth (1:2): a few dozen to perhaps a hundred or so believers, meeting in several households, in a Roman colony of freed slaves, traders and soldiers' families on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese. The church was mostly Gentile, with some Jews (Crispus, 1:14; Acts 18:8). It included a few of means (Gaius, Stephanas, and Erastus, the city treasurer, Romans 16:23) and many of ordinary or low rank (1:26). Paul had founded it and stayed a year and a half (Acts 18:1-18). Apollos worked there next (Acts 18:27-19:1; 1 Corinthians 3:6). Paul knew them well, had sent Timothy (4:17), and had heard from Chloe's people (1:11) and from Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus (16:17). The Corinthians had also written to him (7:1).
audience.why: Paul writes because the church is not behaving as one body. Three things had happened: they were divided into groups around teachers (1:10-4:21); they were tolerating serious sin and lawsuits (5-6) and had questions on marriage, idol meat, worship, gifts and the resurrection (7-15); and some doubted his authority. He answers each in turn, always with the aim of unity and of putting the cross of Christ at the center. Knowing the audience changes the reading. Corinth was a city of status and display, so the Corinthian pride in wisdom, gifts and freedom is a local one. Paul's answers are given to this church and its habits, not as general rules for every place. When we read "women be silent" (14:34) or "all things are lawful" (6:12), we need first to ask what they were answering. At the same time Paul says he teaches the same ways "in every church" (4:17; 7:17; 14:33), so some of his instructions are meant to apply widely. Churches differ on which these are.
views: Most scholars hold that the church was mostly Gentile, with a Jewish minority from the synagogue (Crispus, Sosthenes). Paul addresses them as people who once were pagans (12:2) and treats the Scripture as authority they know.

A few scholars stress the number of Jewish members from the synagogue and think the church had a stronger Jewish element than commonly assumed, since Paul uses so much Scripture. The text of the letter itself favors a Gentile majority.

outline: Divisions: the cross and human wisdom; servants and stewards; Paul as father
Sexual immorality and lawsuits: the man and his father's wife; the lawsuit; "all things are lawful"; the body and the Spirit
Marriage, divorce, the unmarried, slavery, the present distress
Food offered to idols; Paul's rights; Israel in the wilderness; freedom and love
Spiritual gifts: one body; the way of love; tongues and prophecy; order in worship
The resurrection of Christ and of the dead
The collection, travel plans, greetings, "Our Lord, come"

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter against Corinth: a Roman colony rebuilt in 44 BC, the Isthmian Games, patronage and status, the households of Chloe, Stephanas, Gaius and Crispus, Erastus the city treasurer, Gallio's inscription at Delphi for the date, Paul writing from Ephesus. Used by historians such as Jerome Murphy-O'Connor, Gerd Theissen, Wayne Meeks and Bruce Winter.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made: the earlier lost letter (5:9), the unity of the letter against the partition theories, possible later additions (11:3-16; 14:34-35), the slogans where Paul may quote the Corinthians (6:12; 7:1; 8:1, 4), and the manuscripts (Papyrus 46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Claromontanus, the Western text).

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's design: Margaret Mitchell's reading of it as deliberative rhetoric appealing for unity, the shape of chapters 8-10 and of 12-14 with chapter 13 at its center, the rhetoric of irony and hardship lists, and Paul's use of Scripture.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Paul as a Jew writing to a mostly Gentile church: his use of Torah (the Passover at 5:7-8, Deuteronomy 25:4 at 9:9, the exodus in chapter 10, Isaiah 28:11-12 at 14:21), the Shema in 8:6, the stumbling block of a crucified Messiah, and readings by Jewish scholars (Boyarin, Fredriksen, Nanos) and the Paul-within-Judaism school.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows how the churches have read the letter: Chrysostom's homilies, Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, the Council of Trent and the Reformation debates over the Lord's Supper (11:23-29) and the resurrection, Orthodox readings (theosis, the liturgy), and modern Pentecostal and charismatic readings of chapters 12-14.

sections.b:
The letter is a bundle of answers. Paul takes up one problem after another, and many of the problems come from the Corinthians' own letter. When he begins "Now about ..." (7:1, 25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1, 12), he is answering one of their questions. When he writes "I hear that ..." (1:11; 5:1; 11:18), he is answering a report. Reading it well means asking each time what the Corinthians had said, done or asked.

Paul sometimes seems to quote the Corinthians and then answer: the saying about everything being lawful (6:12), "it is good for a man not to touch a woman" (7:1), "we all have knowledge" (8:1). Scholars disagree on where such quotations are, since the Greek has no quotation marks, and this affects how some of the hardest passages read. Each is treated where it comes.

Key words are given one English each time in this Plain: wisdom (sophia), flesh (sarx), spiritual (pneumatikos), love (agape), church (ekklesia), brothers (adelphoi), servant (diakonos), steward (oikonomos), boast (kauchaomai), bring to nothing (katargeo).

Old Corinth was destroyed by Rome in 146 BC. Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC, and it grew fast: two harbors, the Isthmian Games, and a mix of freed slaves, traders and veterans. It was the seat of the Roman governor of Achaia.

Paul arrived from Athens, stayed in the home of Aquila and Priscilla, tentmakers, preached first in the synagogue, and then next door in the house of Titius Justus (Acts 18:1-11). He remained a year and a half. In his time the Jews brought him before the governor Gallio, who is named as proconsul in a letter of Claudius found at Delphi and dated to AD 52 (Acts 18:12-17). Paul later wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, then visited, and wrote more (2 Corinthians).

The Corinthian correspondence is more tangled than the titles suggest. Paul's "previous letter" (1 Corinthians 5:9) is lost. Our 1 Corinthians answers the Corinthians' own letter (7:1) and the report of Chloe's people. Later came a painful visit and a "tearful letter" (2 Corinthians 2:1-4; 7:8), also lost or possibly part of 2 Corinthians 10-13, and then our 2 Corinthians, which some think combines several letters. All of this shows a continuing, often hard, relationship in which Paul's authority was challenged.

sections.h: Paul and Torah in this letter
sections.b: Paul writes as a Jew to a mostly Gentile church, and he assumes they have learned the Scriptures. In chapters 1-4 he quotes Isaiah, Jeremiah, Job and the Psalms, and calls the church God's field, God's building and God's temple, Old Testament pictures of Israel. Later he reads the Passover into the church's life (5:7-8), Deuteronomy 25:4 into the apostle's right to support (9:9), and the exodus into a warning (10:1-13). Jewish and Christian scholars differ on how far Paul keeps the Torah's commandments for Gentiles: the "Paul within Judaism" scholars (Nanos, Fredriksen, Gager) read Paul as a Jew who stayed within Judaism rather than leaving it, while earlier Christian readings stress Paul's break with the Law. This letter does not settle the question, but it shows Paul using Scripture as authority every time.

The oldest manuscript of 1 Corinthians is Papyrus 46 (about AD 200), which holds most of Paul's letters. Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), Alexandrinus (400s), Ephraemi (400s) and Claromontanus (a Greek-Latin manuscript of the 500s, the main Western witness in Paul) are the other main Greek witnesses, with the Old Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions and the church fathers. Most differences are small. The best-known questions in chapters 1-4 are whether Paul wrote "you were baptized" or "I baptized" (1:15), "testimony" or "mystery" (2:1), and "strife" or "strife and dissensions" (3:3). Elsewhere in the letter the ones that matter most are the place of 14:34-35 and the wording of 15:51. Each is treated at its verse.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the letter is built around "the Day"
spec.body: The Day of the Lord appears at the opening (1:8, "blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ"), in the middle of the first section (3:13, "the Day will make it clear") and in the judgment on the man in chapter 5 (5:5), and again at the climax of the letter (15:23-28, 50-57). It may be that Paul sets every argument, however practical, under that Day: how they treat teachers, sinners, food and worship will be shown on it. This is my own suggestion; scholars have noted the letter's end-time frame, but I have not seen this pattern argued in this form, and it rests on reading 5:5 and 15:23-28 as part of the same frame.

prompts:
A scribe's room in a harbor city of the Roman East: Paul, a lean middle-aged man in a plain tunic and cloak, paces and speaks with one hand raised; a young scribe writes on a long papyrus sheet at a low table; Chloe's messengers wait by the door, travel-stained, with a bundle of scrolls; an oil lamp burns; through an open window are masts and the columns of a theater.

Style: sketched by hand onto a weathered papyrus scroll, ink and faded earth colors, ancient manuscript with cave-drawing figures and a few modern line-art strokes, soft torn edges, no hard rectangle.

A crowded courtyard room in a merchant's house in Corinth: a few well-dressed men reclining near a table, many poorer people standing or sitting on the floor, a woman reading from a papyrus roll, children at the back; the walls are painted plaster and a lamp hangs from the beam; the air is tense, with small groups turned away from one another.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old scroll, ink and ochre washes, ancient manuscript, cave-drawing figures and modern line art mixed, soft torn edges, no hard rectangle.

A Roman arena at midday from the side of the crowd: a line of ragged, thin men in worn tunics led out last onto the sand, hands bound, looking up; on the seats, rows of faces turn toward them, and above them in the sky, faint outlines of angels watching.

Style: sketched by hand onto a scroll, charcoal and ink, ancient manuscript with cave-drawing figures and modern line art, soft edges, no hard rectangle.

traditions.q: How far do Paul's instructions in 1 Corinthians bind every church today?
views: Scripture and Tradition together are interpreted by the Church's living teaching office, not by each reader alone (Dei Verbum 9-10). That office decides how Paul's instructions apply to the church today.
The letter is read within the Church's living Tradition, which Orthodox teaching sees as interpreting Scripture through the Fathers, the councils and worship.

Scripture is the only rule: the whole counsel of God is either set down in Scripture or follows from it by good and necessary consequence, and some circumstances of worship and church government are ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence (Westminster Confession 1.6).

The Bible is the supreme standard by which all human conduct, creeds and religious opinions should be tried, and each local church is self-governing (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, articles 1 and 6). Baptists have differed on how to apply passages such as those on women and on the gifts.
Pentecostal churches teach that the gifts of chapters 12-14 have not ceased and are meant for the church in every age.
The Schleitheim Confession puts baptism of those who have repented, the ban (excommunication) and the breaking of bread among the first marks of a gathered church of believers.
